f1.title: Punch Your First Deck
f1.story: Your very first job on the IBM 704. The operator takes your deck, and twenty minutes later the printout lands in your mailbox.
f1.task: Print IBM 704 on the first line and FORTRAN 1957 on the second. Use one WRITE and one FORMAT per line. End the deck with STOP and END.

requirements.message: Use one WRITE for each line.
The last card has to be END.

hints: WRITE (6,10) prints the line described by FORMAT number 10.
10 FORMAT (' IBM 704'): don't forget the blank at the start, it's eaten by the printer.
Then a second WRITE (6,20) with its own FORMAT 20, and STOP and END at the end.

f2.title: The Average
f2.story: A physics teacher has three measurements: 7, 8 and 8 seconds. The computer must print their average with two decimals. Last week's program printed 7.00. Oops.
f2.task: Compute the average of 7, 8 and 8 and print it with two decimals (7.67). Avoid the integer division trap!

requirements.message: Let the computer divide by 3.
Print the result with an F format and two decimals, like F6.2.

hints: If you add integers, the sum is an integer, and dividing by 3 cuts off the decimals.
Use REAL numbers: X = (7. + 8. + 8.) / 3. Or FLOAT(ISUM) / 3.
WRITE (6,10) X with 10 FORMAT (1X, F6.2).

f3.title: The Price List
f3.story: The university shop wants a printed price list, with the item numbers and prices lined up neatly.
f3.task: Print this table exactly: a header ITEM PRICE, then items 1 to 3 with the prices 2.50, 12.75 and 0.99. Use FORMAT (1X, I4, F8.2) for the item lines.

requirements.message: Use FORMAT (1X, I4, F8.2) for the item lines.

hints: The header: 10 FORMAT (' ITEM   PRICE'). The blank at the start is for the printer.
One FORMAT for all item lines: 20 FORMAT (1X, I4, F8.2).
WRITE (6,20) 1, 2.50 works, but nicer: put the price in a variable first, like P = 2.50.

fc1-project.title: The Circle Calculator
fc1-project.story: An engineer needs the measurements of a pipe with a radius of 2.5 cm, printed with labels, for the workshop.
fc1-project.task: For R = 2.5, compute the area (pi × R²) and the circumference (2 × pi × R), with pi = 3.14159. Print three lines: RADIUS, AREA and CIRCUMFERENCE, each followed by its value with two decimals.

requirements.message: Square the radius in your formula, like R ** 2.
Print the values with two decimals, like F8.2.

hints: PI = 3.14159, R = 2.5, then A = PI * R ** 2 and C = 2. * PI * R.
One FORMAT can print all three lines: 10 FORMAT (' RADIUS', F12.2/' AREA', F14.2/' CIRCUMFERENCE', F6.2).
Or three WRITEs, each with its own FORMAT. Don't forget STOP and END.

f4.title: Countdown
f4.story: Cape Canaveral, 1962. The launch computer has to count down from 5 and then give the signal. DO loops can't count backwards, so the engineers do it the old way.
f4.task: Print 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, each on its own line, then LIFTOFF. Build the loop by hand with GO TO and the three-way IF.

requirements.message: Use the three-way IF, like IF (K) 10, 20, 30.

hints: Start with K = 5. Print K, then K = K - 1.
IF (K) 30, 30, 10 jumps back to 10 while K is still positive, and goes on to 30 at zero.
At 30, write LIFTOFF with its own FORMAT. Don't forget STOP and END.

f5.title: Leap Years
f5.story: The calendar office wants a list of leap years. The rule: a year divisible by 4 is a leap year, except years divisible by 100, unless they are also divisible by 400. That's why 1900 wasn't one.
f5.task: Check every year from 1896 to 1904 and print only the leap years. Loop with a counter and GO TO, and test the rule with MOD, .AND. and .OR.

requirements.message: Test divisibility with MOD, like MOD(IY, 4) .EQ. 0.
Combine the rule with .AND. or .OR.

hints: IY = 1896 to start. At the end of the loop: IY = IY + 1, then IF (IY .LE. 1904) GO TO 10.
Divisible by 4 and not by 100: MOD(IY, 4) .EQ. 0 .AND. MOD(IY, 100) .NE. 0.
Add the 400 rule with .OR.: IF (… .OR. MOD(IY, 400) .EQ. 0) WRITE (6,20) IY, with 20 FORMAT (1X, I4).

f6.title: The Times Table
f6.story: A school in 1965 orders printed times tables from the university computer: one neat sheet per class.
f6.task: Print the times table from 1 to 5: five lines, each with the numbers I, 2×I, 3×I, 4×I and 5×I. Use a DO loop and FORMAT (1X, 5I4).

requirements.message: Use a DO loop.
Use FORMAT (1X, 5I4) to line the numbers up.

hints: DO 10 I = 1, 5 with a CONTINUE numbered 10.
One WRITE per line, with five values: WRITE (6,20) I, 2*I, 3*I, 4*I, 5*I.
20 FORMAT (1X, 5I4) gives each number four columns.

fc2-project.title: The Prime Finder
fc2-project.story: Mathematicians used early computers to hunt for prime numbers, numbers that can only be divided by 1 and themselves. Your job: find all of them up to 50.
fc2-project.task: Print every prime number from 2 to 50, one per line. For each N, try the divisors 2 up to N - 1 with MOD. If one divides evenly, N isn't prime.

requirements.message: Use two DO loops: one for N, one for the divisors.
Test the divisors with MOD.

hints: 2 is the only even prime: print it first, then let N run from 3 to 50.
Before the inner loop, set M = N - 1. Then DO 10 K = 2, M, and inside: IF (MOD(N, K) .EQ. 0) GO TO 30.
After the inner loop's CONTINUE, WRITE N. Number the outer loop's CONTINUE 30, so a divisor jumps past the WRITE.

f7.title: The Warmest Day
f7.story: The weather service logged a week of noon temperatures: 12.5, 15.0, 17.5, 21.0, 19.5, 16.0 and 14.5 degrees. Which day was the warmest?
f7.task: Store the seven temperatures in an array T(7). Find the highest one with a DO loop and print the day and the temperature, like DAY 4 21.0.
f7.starter:
C     THE WARMEST DAY
      DIMENSION T(7)

requirements.message: Keep the temperatures in an array with DIMENSION T(7).
Find the maximum with a DO loop.

hints: Set T(1) = 12.5, T(2) = 15.0 … one card each.
Start with BIG = T(1) and IDAY = 1, then DO 10 I = 2, 7.
Inside the loop: IF (T(I) .GT. BIG) IDAY = I, then IF (T(I) .GT. BIG) BIG = T(I). Print with FORMAT (' DAY', I2, F6.1).

f8.title: The Class Average
f8.story: A teacher brings a stack of data cards: one test score per card, columns 1–4, and a last card with -1. The office wants the number of students and the average.
f8.task: Read scores until the -1 card. Print STUDENTS with the count, then AVERAGE with one decimal.

requirements.message: Read the scores with READ (5, …).

hints: Loop: 10 READ (5,20) K with 20 FORMAT (I4), then IF (K .LT. 0) GO TO 30.
Count with N = N + 1 and add with ISUM = ISUM + K, then GO TO 10.
At 30: AVG = FLOAT(ISUM) / FLOAT(N). Watch out for the integer division trap! Print with FORMAT (' STUDENTS', I3/' AVERAGE', F6.1).

f9.title: The Square Root Table
f9.story: Before pocket calculators, engineers looked up square roots in printed tables. Your computer center sells them.
f9.task: Print a header line N SQRT(N), then the numbers 1 to 5 with their square roots to 4 decimals. Use FORMAT (1X, I4, F10.4) for the number lines.

requirements.message: Use the built-in SQRT function.
Use FORMAT (1X, I4, F10.4) for the number lines.

hints: Header: 10 FORMAT ('    N   SQRT(N)'). The first blank is eaten by the printer.
DO 20 N = 1, 5. SQRT needs a REAL: X = SQRT(FLOAT(N)).
WRITE (6,30) N, X with 30 FORMAT (1X, I4, F10.4).

fc3-project.title: The Weather Station
fc3-project.story: A weather station sends a week of readings on seven data cards, one temperature per card in columns 1–6. The meteorologist wants a report.
fc3-project.task: Read the seven temperatures into an array. Print the average, the highest and the lowest temperature, each with one decimal: AVERAGE, HIGHEST and LOWEST.
fc3-project.starter:
C     THE WEATHER STATION
      DIMENSION T(7)

requirements.message: Keep the readings in an array.
Read the data cards with READ (5, …).
Use a DO loop to go through the readings.

hints: READ (5,10) (T(I), I = 1, 7) with 10 FORMAT (F6.1) reads one card per value: the format is used again for each card.
SUM = 0.0, BIG = T(1), SMALL = T(1). Then DO 20 I = 1, 7: add T(I), and compare with BIG and SMALL using logical IFs.
Print with FORMAT (' AVERAGE', F6.1/' HIGHEST', F6.1/' LOWEST', F7.1), and AVERAGE = SUM / 7.0.

f10.title: Factorials
f10.story: A statistics professor needs factorials: 5! = 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 × 5 = 120. She wants a table from 1 to 6, and a function she can reuse.
f10.task: Write FUNCTION IFACT(N) that works out N!. In the main program, print N and IFACT(N) for N = 1 to 6, one pair per line.

requirements.message: Write the factorial as FUNCTION IFACT(N).
Use IFACT(N) in the main program.

hints: Main program: DO 10 N = 1, 6, then WRITE (6,20) N, IFACT(N) with 20 FORMAT (1X, I3, I6).
After the main END: FUNCTION IFACT(N), then IFACT = 1.
DO 10 I = 1, N with IFACT = IFACT * I inside, then RETURN and END.

f11.title: Sort the Scores
f11.story: The sports club punched six race times in seconds: 72, 85, 64, 90, 77 and 58. The results board needs them from fastest to slowest.
f11.task: Put the six times in an integer array, sort it in SUBROUTINE ISORT(K, N) and print them on one line with FORMAT (1X, 6I4).
f11.starter:
C     SORT THE SCORES
      DIMENSION K(6)
      K(1) = 72
      K(2) = 85
      K(3) = 64
      K(4) = 90
      K(5) = 77
      K(6) = 58

requirements.message: Sort in SUBROUTINE ISORT(K, N).
CALL ISORT from the main program.

hints: Main program: CALL ISORT(K, 6), then WRITE (6,10) K with 10 FORMAT (1X, 6I4).
SUBROUTINE ISORT(K, N) with DIMENSION K(N). Use the SORT from the lesson, but with integers: the spare variable must be an integer too, like M.
Inside the two loops: IF (K(J) .GE. K(I)) GO TO 10, then M = K(I), K(I) = K(J), K(J) = M.

f12.title: The Price Calculator
f12.story: The university shop changes its tax rate now and then. The prices are fixed, so they go in a DATA card, and the tax rate is shared through COMMON.
f12.task: Prices 2.50, 12.75 and 0.99 in a DATA statement. Set the tax rate to 0.20 in the main program and share it with COMMON. A subroutine prints each price with tax, two decimals per line.

requirements.message: Put the prices in a DATA statement.
Share the tax rate with COMMON in the main program and in the subroutine.
Print the prices in a subroutine.

hints: DIMENSION P(3), DATA P / 2.50, 12.75, 0.99 /, COMMON RATE, RATE = 0.20.
DO 10 I = 1, 3 with CALL GROSS(P(I)) inside.
SUBROUTINE GROSS(X) with COMMON R. Then Q = X * (1.0 + R) and WRITE (6,10) Q with 10 FORMAT (1X, F8.2).

fc4-project.title: The Statistics Library
fc4-project.story: A lab has eight measurements and wants a little library of reusable statistics routines, the way SHARE members swapped them in the 1950s.
fc4-project.task: Keep the values 4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42, 7 and 9 in a DATA statement. Write FUNCTION AVG(X, N) and SUBROUTINE MINMAX(X, N, SMALL, BIG). Print AVERAGE, LOWEST, HIGHEST and RANGE (highest minus lowest), each with one decimal.
fc4-project.starter:
C     THE STATISTICS LIBRARY
      DIMENSION A(8)

requirements.message: Put the measurements in a DATA statement.
Write FUNCTION AVG(X, N).
Write SUBROUTINE MINMAX(X, N, SMALL, BIG).

hints: DATA A / 4., 8., 15., 16., 23., 42., 7., 9. /. Then CALL MINMAX(A, 8, S, B) and WRITE (6,10) AVG(A, 8), S, B, B - S.
10 FORMAT (' AVERAGE', F6.1/' LOWEST', F6.1/' HIGHEST', F6.1/' RANGE', F6.1).
MINMAX: SMALL = X(1), BIG = X(1), then a DO loop with IF (X(I) .LT. SMALL) SMALL = X(I) and the same for BIG.

f13.title: The Square Root of 10
f13.story: 1957: the IBM 704 at the university gets a new job. A physicist needs the square root of 10 to five decimals, and wants to see that Newton's method can do it without the library.
f13.task: Find the square root of 10 with Newton's method, starting from X = 1.0. Repeat until the change is smaller than 1.0E-6, then print the result with five decimals.

requirements.message: Stop when ABS(XNEW - X) is small enough.
Use Newton's step: (X + A / X) / 2.

hints: IF (ABS(XNEW - X) .LT. 1.0E-6) GO TO 20, otherwise X = XNEW and GO TO 10.
At 20: WRITE (6,30) XNEW with 30 FORMAT (1X, F10.5).

f14.title: The Best Angle
f14.story: An artillery officer asks: at 50 m/s, how far does a shell fly at different angles? Without air, the physics is exact: flight time T = 2 × VY / 9.81, distance = VX × T.
f14.task: For the angles 15, 30, 45, 60 and 75 degrees, print the angle and the distance with one decimal. Use a DO loop with a step of 15, and convert to radians with 3.14159.

requirements.message: Loop over the angles with DO … = 15, 75, 15.
Split the speed with SIN and COS.

hints: DO 10 IDEG = 15, 75, 15, then RAD = FLOAT(IDEG) * 3.14159 / 180.0.
VX = 50.0 * COS(RAD), VY = 50.0 * SIN(RAD), T = 2.0 * VY / 9.81, D = VX * T.
WRITE (6,20) IDEG, D with 20 FORMAT (1X, I3, F8.1). Notice which angles give the same distance!

f15.title: The Area Under a Sine
f15.story: The area under one arch of the sine curve, from 0 to π, is exactly 2. A good check for your trapezoid program.
f15.task: Use the trapezoid rule with N = 100 strips to work out the area under SIN(X) from 0 to 3.14159. Print it with four decimals.
f15.starter: C     THE AREA UNDER A SINE

requirements.message: Integrate SIN(X).
Count the two end points half: (F(A) + F(B)) / 2.

hints: SUM = (SIN(0.0) + SIN(PI)) / 2.0, then DO 10 I = 1, 99 with SUM = SUM + SIN(FLOAT(I) * H).
SUM = SUM * H, then WRITE with FORMAT (1X, F8.4). It's just below 2: why?

fc5-project.title: Computing Pi
fc5-project.story: A quarter circle with radius 1 has the area π/4. Its curve is Y = SQRT(1 - X²). In 1949, ENIAC computed π to 2037 digits. You'll settle for a table that shows how the trapezoid rule closes in on it.
fc5-project.task: Compute 4 × the area under SQRT(1 - X**2) from 0 to 1 with the trapezoid rule, for N = 10, 100 and 1000 strips. Print N and the result with five decimals on each line.

requirements.message: The quarter circle is SQRT(1.0 - X ** 2).
Use one loop for N and one for the strips.

hints: The end points are known: F(0) = 1 and F(1) = 0, so start with SUM = (1.0 + 0.0) / 2.0. That also avoids SQRT of a tiny negative number at X = 1.
N = 10, then DO 30 K = 1, 3. Inside: H = 1.0 / FLOAT(N), M = N - 1, and DO 20 I = 1, M with X = FLOAT(I) * H and SUM = SUM + SQRT(1.0 - X ** 2).
PI = 4.0 * SUM * H. Print with FORMAT (1X, I5, F10.5), then N = N * 10.

f16.title: The Leap Year Function
f16.story: The Gregorian calendar has a tricky rule: every 4th year is a leap year, but not every 100th, unless it's a 400th. A perfect logical function.
f16.task: Write LOGICAL FUNCTION LEAP(IY). Then print each of the years 1900, 1957, 1960, 2000 and 2100 with T or F for leap year, using an I5 and an L3 field.

requirements.message: Write LOGICAL FUNCTION LEAP(IY).
Declare LOGICAL LEAP in the main program too.
Print the answer with an L format.

hints: LEAP = (MOD(IY, 4) .EQ. 0 .AND. MOD(IY, 100) .NE. 0) .OR. MOD(IY, 400) .EQ. 0
Keep the years in an array: DIMENSION IYS(5) with DATA IYS /1900, 1957, 1960, 2000, 2100/.
WRITE (6,20) IYS(I), LEAP(IYS(I)) with 20 FORMAT (1X, I5, L3).

f17.title: The Roots of x² + 2x + 5
f17.story: An engineer's circuit gives the equation x² + 2x + 5 = 0. Its discriminant is negative, so the roots are complex: a job for FORTRAN's COMPLEX type.
f17.task:
Use the formula x = (-B ± √(B² - 4AC)) / 2A with A = 1, B = 2, C = 5. Compute the square root with CSQRT, and print both roots, each with its real and imaginary part, as F6.2 fields:
 -1.00  2.00
 -1.00 -2.00
f17.starter:
C     COMPLEX ROOTS
      COMPLEX R, X1, X2

requirements.message: Use COMPLEX variables.
Take the square root with CSQRT.
Make a complex value with CMPLX.

hints: R = CSQRT(CMPLX(DISC, 0.0)) gives 0 + 4i.
X1 = (CMPLX(-B, 0.0) + R) / (2.0 * A), X2 the same with -. Then WRITE (6,10) X1 with 10 FORMAT (1X, 2F6.2).

f18.title: The Vowel Counter
f18.story: A linguist wants to know how many vowels a line of text has. She brings a deck of cards, but you only need to handle the first one.
f18.task:
Read a 40-column card with 40A1. Count how many letters are A, E, I, O or U (keep the vowels in an array filled by DATA), and print the count and the card again:
 7 VOWELS IN: PROGRAMMING IN FORTRAN IV
f18.starter:
C     THE VOWEL COUNTER
      INTEGER C(40), V(5)
f18.expectedOutput: 7 VOWELS IN: PROGRAMMING IN FORTRAN IV

requirements.message: Read one character per element with A1.
Fill the vowels in with DATA.
Compare letters with .EQ..

hints: DATA V /1HA, 1HE, 1HI, 1HO, 1HU/
Two DO loops: for each of the 40 letters, check all 5 vowels.
WRITE (6,30) N, C with 30 FORMAT (1X, I2, ' VOWELS IN: ', 40A1).

fc6-project.title: The Equation Desk
fc6-project.story: 1965: the engineering department sends a deck of cards, each with a name and three coefficients. Your program solves every equation, real or complex.
fc6-project.task: Each card has a name in columns 1-4 (A4), then A, B and C (3F6.1). For each of the three cards, solve Ax² + Bx + C = 0. Use a LOGICAL variable REALRT that is .TRUE. when B² - 4AC is not negative. Print the name and T or F, then the two roots: as real numbers (F8.2) if REALRT, otherwise as complex numbers (each as two F8.2 fields).
fc6-project.starter:
C     THE EQUATION DESK
      INTEGER NAME
      LOGICAL REALRT
      COMPLEX R, X1, X2

requirements.message: Use a LOGICAL variable for the kind of roots.
Use COMPLEX for the complex roots.
Read the name with A4.
Print the logical value with an L format.

hints: READ (5,10) NAME, A, B, C with 10 FORMAT (A4, 3F6.1), inside DO 50 K = 1, 3.
DISC = B ** 2 - 4.0 * A * C, REALRT = DISC .GE. 0.0, and WRITE (6,20) NAME, REALRT with 20 FORMAT (1X, A4, L2).
IF (REALRT) GO TO 30. Complex: R = CSQRT(CMPLX(DISC, 0.0)), X1 = (CMPLX(-B, 0.0) + R) / (2.0 * A), and X2 with -. Real: X1 = (-B + SQRT(DISC)) / (2.0 * A).
